title: The global economy has been resilient — so far
gist: World Bank Prospects Group economists argue the global economy has withstood the 2026 Strait of Hormuz oil shock (Brent near $120) with 2026 consensus growth still about 2.6%, thanks to fast energy-market adjustment, rapid policy support, AI capex and stronger EMDE policy frameworks. But inflation forecasts have risen 0.8pp to 3.4%, long-term yields are up, and EMDEs outside China and India face slowing growth, debt vulnerabilities and a lost decade of convergence.

themes.theme: Hormuz oil shock and market reaction

insights.claim: Disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz in 2026 briefly drove Brent crude to nearly $120 a barrel, roughly two-thirds above its price on the eve of the Middle East conflict, yet the global economy avoided the steep downturn historically associated with such oil shocks.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Oil-shock-to-recession playbooks have underperformed this cycle; the economy's oil intensity and buffers appear to have dulled the transmission.

insights.claim: Oil prices retreated to near pre-conflict levels by end-June 2026 as fears eased, but have since again approached the conflict-start highs as ongoing closures of the Strait of Hormuz sharply reduced shipments.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Energy price risk is two-sided and regime-dependent on Hormuz status; the June relief proved temporary.

insights.claim: Equities rebounded strongly after the April 8 ceasefire, lifted in advanced economies by AI optimism, with gains spreading to many emerging markets, while energy importers dependent on Middle Eastern supply and economies with pre-existing vulnerabilities recovered more slowly.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Dispersion within EM: commodity exporters outside the conflict zone and strong-framework countries saw sovereign spreads recover fastest — a cross-sectional EM credit signal.

insights.so_what: The shock has been primarily an inflation shock rather than a growth shock so far — a stagflation-lite mix that argues against expecting rapid rate cuts.

insights.claim: Growth in EMDEs excluding China and India is forecast to slow from 3.0% in 2025 to 2.5% in 2026, about 0.4 percentage point below January expectations, while East Asia and Pacific and South Asia are tracking in line with or above January forecasts.

insights.so_what: Headline EM resilience masks weakness in the smaller EMDEs; Asia is the relative winner, conflict-affected economies the losers.

insights.claim: Because higher energy prices hit consumer bills quickly but affect activity with a lag as households cut spending and firms rethink investment, the small revision to global growth forecasts may understate the downside risk if energy prices stay high.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Growth downgrades may still be coming in 2027 if oil stays elevated; consensus may be too sanguine.

insights.claim: World Bank economists identify four factors that kept the 2026 oil shock from causing a deeper downturn: fast energy-market adjustment, quick government action, AI investment as an engine of demand, and stronger EMDE policy frameworks.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Each pillar is a monitorable variable — inventories, fiscal space, AI capex, and EM institutional credibility; erosion of any weakens the resilience case.
insights.quote: Four factors have made the difference.

insights.claim: Energy markets adjusted rapidly because inventories were drawn down, producers outside the conflict region raised exports, and weaker demand in several major economies limited the oil price rise.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Inventory buffers have been partly spent, so a second disruption would meet thinner cushions.
insights.locator: First, energy markets adjusted rapidly

insights.claim: Governments and businesses responded by conserving energy, releasing strategic reserves and switching to alternatives including renewables and coal, while many developing economies introduced fuel subsidies and price caps that gave relief but strained public finances.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Short-term demand support for coal and renewables; subsidies widen EM fiscal deficits.
insights.locator: Second, governments acted quickly

insights.claim: The World Bank Group made $50–60 billion available to protect vulnerable households, strengthen public finances and provide capital and liquidity to businesses, and can scale this to $80–100 billion over 15 months if conditions deteriorate.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A multilateral backstop of up to $100bn limits tail risk for vulnerable sovereigns' financing.

insights.claim: Large-scale AI capital spending in the United States has become a powerful engine of global demand, spilling over to East Asian EMDEs through strong demand for electronics and AI infrastructure inputs, visible in global electronics manufacturing PMIs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Global growth resilience is partly hostage to the AI capex cycle; an AI spending slowdown would remove a key shock absorber, especially for Asian electronics exporters.
insights.quote: AI investment became a powerful engine of global demand.

insights.claim: More EMDEs now use inflation targets and fiscal rules than in earlier shocks, and many have larger FX reserves, deeper local capital markets and more credible central banks, which helped them retain investor confidence.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Supports differentiating EM exposure by institutional quality; framework strength explained faster spread recovery.

themes.theme: Debt vicious cycle and lost convergence

insights.claim: Successive shocks — the pandemic, supply disruptions, the inflation surge and geopolitical tensions — have depleted fiscal buffers and raised debt in many EMDEs, and rising global interest rates are now making that debt costlier to refinance and service.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Refinancing walls in frontier sovereigns are the key fragility beneath the resilience headline.
insights.locator: 4. What dangers lie beneath

insights.claim: High debt and tighter financing restrict investment, weak investment limits productivity and growth, and slow growth makes debt harder to manage, leaving governments less room to respond to the next crisis — a vicious cycle.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Debt-growth doom loop framework for assessing sovereign credit trajectories in EMDEs.
insights.quote: The result can be a vicious cycle.

insights.claim: By 2028, EMDEs excluding China and India are on track to have lost nearly a decade of income convergence with advanced economies, and many fragile and conflict-affected countries are falling further behind.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Structural underperformance of the broader EM ex-China/India universe argues against assuming catch-up growth.

insights.claim: An estimated 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in EMDEs over the next decade, more than one-fifth of them in economies affected by fragility and conflict.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Demographics are either a growth dividend or a destabilizing force depending on job creation — a long-run political-risk driver.

insights.claim: The World Bank economists set three policy priorities: protect vulnerable households with targeted, temporary support; make careful fiscal and monetary choices to stop the energy shock becoming persistent inflation while rebuilding buffers; and boost investment, productivity and job creation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Signals multilateral pressure against broad untargeted fuel subsidies and in favour of fiscal consolidation and private-capital mobilization.

insights.claim: The authors warn that past resilience does not guarantee future results and urge policymakers to use the current period to rebuild economic strength before the next shock arrives.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The institutional message is caution, not complacency — the authors see buffers as depleted.
